articles.title_orig: Nvidia scrutiny raises questions over U.S. chip exports, China and national security
articles.title_zh: Nvidia scrutiny raises questions over U.S. chip exports, China and national security
articles.content_orig:
Singapore, a hub for billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia sales each year, finds itself increasingly in the crosshairs of Washington's push to stop advanced AI chips from reaching China, as the chipmaker CEO's scandal once again thrusts the city-state into the spotlight.
The Southeast Asian nation said Thursday that it had barred Alice Huang, the businesswoman at the center of a scandal that catalyzed the end of Jensen Huang's run as Nvidia CEO, from re-entering the country.
A fifth person was handed 41 charges on Friday in a Singapore fraud case involving computer servers that might have contained Nvidia chips and were exported to Malaysia. The alleged transactions in the broader case totaled about $390 million, prosecutors said March last year.
The investigations into several companies and key officials, including Megaspeed International, began in February 2025 and remained ongoing as of Thursday.
Authorities have been examining whether servers exported through Singapore to Malaysia without entering the domestic market were subsequently rerouted to another destination, contrary to declarations made in Singapore, the Ministry of Home Affairs said in a statement late Thursday.
Singapore has faced growing international scrutiny, particularly from the U.S., over its role as a major billing and potential transit hub for Nvidia chips that U.S. officials say have reached China.
The U.S. has imposed export restrictions on Nvidia's most cutting-edge AI chips to China since 2022 to curb Beijing's surging AI development.
Nvidia's revenue linked to Singapore rose to 22% in the fiscal quarter ending July 2025, up from 8% in 2023, with the country's trade ministry estimating chips physically delivered there accounted for less than 1% of the chipmaker's revenue.
Experts have pointed to gaps in enforcement of U.S. export restrictions and Singapore's corporate system that make it hard to trace where advanced Nvidia chips ultimately end up.
Nvidia chips can be legally sold to customers in other countries, such as Malaysia or Singapore, and then illicitly resold or re-exported to China. Chinese companies can also legally gain remote access to the most advanced AI chips hosted in data centers outside China rather than buying the hardware directly.
Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at Council on Foreign Relations and former U.S. national security official, said that Southeast Asia has become "a major hub for chip smuggling and export control circumvention," importing tens of billions of dollars' worth of AI chips per year.
Singapore has stepped up efforts to police suspected chip diversion since last year, including investigations involving alleged fraud and money laundering.
Authorities acknowledged the potential "blind spots between separate monitoring of trade flows and banking flows," said Alvin Camba, lead scientist and director of research at Lyvi, an Austin-based AI risk assessment firm. Correlating physical shipments with related financial transactions can be "challenging," he added.
"Singapore's strong corporate secrecy regulations, which offer extensive protections for foreign investors, can also make it difficult to rapidly identify the true recipients of goods," Camba said.
Those challenges can be exploited to "obfuscate financial flows and potentially circumvent global restrictions on technology transfers," he added, urging constant adaptation from regulators.
Singapore said it had received limited help from U.S. authorities in its yearlong investigation.
Police sought information on Super Micro Computer Inc., a U.S. server supplier relevant to the probe, but the company provided limited cooperation, according to the Thursday statement.
The city-state first raised the issue with U.S. authorities in July 2025, and has repeated its request on several occasions since September last year. "Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company," it said.
Police interviewed Alice Huang, a Hong Kong resident who was then Megaspeed's CEO, chairperson and a key controller, in June 2025.
In February 2026, authorities concluded that there was insufficient evidence that she had committed offenses related to the declarations under investigation. She was nonetheless barred from re-entering Singapore after being found providing inaccurate information to downplay her role in Megaspeed.
The country does not enforce "unilateral export controls" imposed by other countries, the ministry said in Thursday's statement, but it expects companies operating there to take foreign export rules into account in their international business activities.
Megaspeed, which was spun off from a Chinese gaming company, became Nvidia's largest Southeast Asian customer in less than three years and has bought more than $4.8 billion worth of its chips since June 2024, according to The New York Times, though the company has denied any wrongdoing.
Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence identified as a Chinese intelligence asset passing information to Beijing, served as managing director at Megaspeed for eight months in 2023 but has reportedly continued to play a leading role at the company.
Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia CEO on Thursday, ending 33 years at the helm after revelations that he had two extramarital affairs, plunging the chipmaker at the heart of the global AI boom into crisis.
Nvidia appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent successor.

articles.title_orig: Stock futures tick higher as Wall Street heads for winning week despite Nvidia woes: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures tick higher as Wall Street heads for winning week despite Nvidia woes: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equity futures were slightly higher Friday, a day after major indexes declined and Nvidia shares fell following the exit of the scandal-hit chipmaker's founder and CEO Jensen Huang.
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average were up 78 points, or 0.2%. S&P 500 futures added 0.2%, and Nasdaq-100 futures advanced 0.1%.
The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq all pulled back on Thursday, led by a 4.3% drop in Nvidia after Huang stepped down from his post following reported extramarital affairs , including a relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy. Analysts told CNBC that Huang's exit could trigger a 20% correction in the stock.
Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress , who's worked at the company for more than a decade, will lead the chipmaker as interim CEO. The company's board is looking both internally and externally for a full-time replacement for Huang.
A jump in oil prices also kept stocks under pressure Thursday after President Donald Trump said in a Truth Social post , "We don't need a deal with Iran." The comment raised concerns that the U.S.-Iran war could drag on further.
Oil prices were little changed on Friday, with West Texas Intermediate crude futures trading above $88 per barrel and Brent crude futures trading above $96.
Another market catalyst awaits on Friday in the form of October's producer price index reading, a measure of wholesale inflation. Economists polled by Dow Jones see headline PPI rising 0.4% on the month and 6.6% from 12 months earlier.
Even with the latest bout of market turbulence, the major averages are heading for weekly advances. The Nasdaq is up 3.2%, while the S&P 500 is on pace for a 2.9% advance. The Dow is poised for a nearly 2% jump. All three indexes are heading for their best weekly performances since early August.
Bitcoin dropped 3% to trade below $70,000 for the first time since August. The largest cryptocurrency by market cap was last at $69,231.05 and was on pace for its sixth consecutive weekly decline.
Nvidia shares rebounded in pre-market trading on Friday, with the stock adding around 2.3% by 5:30 a.m. ET. It followed a decline of just over 4% in Thursday's regular trading session as investors weighed the company's future without its longtime leader Jensen Huang.
More broadly, stocks in the semiconductor space were mixed ahead of the final opening bell of the week.
AMD shares were last seen trading 2.6% lower. Broadcom fell 2.8%, while Intel , Micron and Lam Research each lost around 0.9%.
Amid a volatile week for Nvidia stock, some of its rivals had earlier emerged as potential beneficiaries of the upheaval.
Microsoft shares were 3% lower in premarket trade at 4:35 a.m. ET, as the company's engineers continued to grapple with server issues that caused a widespread outage of its Outlook service, disrupting businesses, governments and the general public around the world.
Outlook was inaccessible via app or browser throughout the Asian business day and into Europe's morning, with related services also impacted. Connectivity issues began around 1 p.m. ET on Thursday, hitting hundreds of thousands of U.S. Microsoft users.
The company said at 4:14 a.m. ET on Friday that it was seeing "early signs of stabilization" but that service would be "variable," and it was working to preserve mail delayed during the recovery process. It added it was not aware if "malicious activity" was the cause of the incident.
Shares of Richemont are on track for their worst day since July 2023, even after the luxury conglomerate posted quarterly earnings ahead of expectations early Friday.
Swiss-listed shares were down 6.8% in morning trading.
Sales rose 13% at constant exchange rates in the quarter ended September, while its important jewellery business, which includes Cartier and Van Cleef, grew 14%.
Results exceeded expectations; however, they marked a slowdown from the previous quarter, when total sales grew by 20% and jewellery grew by 24%.
The luxury sector has seen a prolonged slump amid higher pricing and overall softer demand, especially in China. Richemont said sales in mainland China were down about 3% in the first half of the fiscal year.
Luxury peers LVMH , Gucci-owner Kering and Hermes all traded lower in morning trading Friday.
Nvidia shares were slightly higher in premarket trading on Friday as investors navigate the fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation after reports of at least two affairs.
It follows a wild day for the stock on Thursday, which dropped sharply before recovering to close just over 4% lower.
Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday after The New York Times reported that Huang had a romantic relationship with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia. He was already under scrutiny following an investigation by the board into his relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy.
Reuters reported on Thursday the existence of another affair with an Nvidia employee, which the news agency did not name. Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
Read the full story here .
Treasury yields edged higher on Friday as investor expectations for a December rate hike by the Federal Reserve gathered strength.
The 10-year U.S. Treasury note yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — rose 2 basis points to 5.1271%.
Investors now see a Federal Reserve rate hike next month as a near certainty. Traders are pricing in 100% odds of a rise at the Dec. 9 meeting, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Odds of a 25 basis points hike now stand at almost 87%, with the chance of a 50 basis point increase at around 13%.
Shares of Richemont were 7.2% lower by 8:50 a.m. in London (3:50 a.m. ET), after the Swiss luxury giant released its fiscal first-half earnings on Friday morning.
In the six months to September, the company said sales jumped 16% year-on-year to 12.3 billion euros ($13.6 billion), slightly beating an analyst consensus estimate compiled by LSEG.
Operating profit surged 33% to 3.1 billion euros, while earnings per share rose to 4.29 euros from 3.08 euros in the same period a year earlier.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 was 0.2% in early trading on Friday, with most sectors and all major regional bourses in negative territory.
The Stoxx 600 Technology index fell 0.6% shortly after the opening bell, putting it on track for its second consecutive day of losses.
Chip stocks extended the sell-off that began Thursday ahead of Jensen Huang abdicating his position as Nvidia CEO. Dutch semiconductor equipment makers ASMI and ASML lost around 1.5% in early dealmaking, while Be Semiconductor was 1.1% lower and shares of Germany's Infineon shed 1.8%.
Asia-Pacific markets closed mostly lower Friday, capping off a week dominated by the Nvidia shakeup.
South Korea's Kospi fell 0.98% to close at 5,290.53, while the small-cap Kosdaq was up 0.45% at 699.66.
China's CSI 300 fell 0.68% to 4,016.29, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was 1.6% lower in its final hour of trade.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 dropped 0.71% to end the day at 9,082.2
The exception was Japan's Nikkei 225 , which gained 0.53%, ending at 61,142.35, while the broader Topix rose 0.11% to 3,941.57.
Shares of Japanese sportswear giant Asics tumbled 14.3% on Friday, after the company's earnings disappointed investors.
Revenue for the firm's fiscal third quarter came in at 270.67 billion Japanese yen ($1.69 billion), below an analyst consensus of 279.6 billion yen compiled by LSEG. Operating profit hit 55.1 billion yen, representing a year-on-year rise of 18.4% but falling short of analyst estimates.
Friday's share move was the biggest one-day drop in Asics' share price since Aug. 2024.
A flash poll of members of CNBC's Financial Advisor Council and Financial Advisor 100 on Thursday showed 18 respondents are planning to hold their Nvidia allocations steady in client portfolios.

articles.title_zh: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq futures edge higher as Nvidia tumult deepens
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
US stock futures held steady on Friday as a bumpy week didn't prevent the major averages from pacing for weekly gains.
Futures on the Dow Jones Industrial Average ( YM=F ) rose 0.1%, while those on the S&P 500 ( ES=F ) gained 0.2%. The Nasdaq-100 ( NQ=F ) climbed 0.1%.
While stocks slipped on Thursday, they have largely held firm against a series of tremors from Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang stepping down to rising oil prices and a sell-off in government bonds.
Nvidia stock recovered on Friday as the fallout from Huang's affairs continued to unfold, raising the stakes for the company's third quarter earnings next Tuesday. Investors are debating whether the controversy surrounding the chip giant's former leader implicates the wider artificial intelligence boom that Nvidia has played a central role in building.
Chipmaker sector stocks declined further in premarket trading.
Oil prices were little changed, providing some relief after a spike in prices sparked Thursday's sell-off in bonds. As traders braced for an interest rate hike in December, the 10-year Treasury yield ( ^TNX ) reached 5.10% on Thursday, its highest level since October.
The set up has pressured the price of bitcoin ( BTC ) with the world's largest cryptocurrency tumbling below $70,000 early Friday for the first time in nearly three months.
On the economic calendar, the producer price index readings will provide a gauge of wholesale inflation in October.
The cheapest way for an American company to run AI is a free model made in China. The scandal that just cost Nvidia its CEO could shut off the chips those models depend on, Yahoo Finance's Jared Blikre writes.
Companies are making the switch fast. Duolingo ( DUOL ) co-founder and CEO Luis von Ahn said at Yahoo Finance Invest on Thursday that each AI practice call in his app used to cost about 30 cents. Now it's "less than a cent," he said, "by moving most of this to open weight models ," the kind of AI anyone can download and run for free. Decagon co-founder and CEO Jesse Zhang said new customers at his AI startup run "almost entirely" on them.
The most downloaded of those free models come from China, and the biggest maker by far is Alibaba ( BABA ).
Jensen Huang is out. The former CEO of Nvidia resigned after a rapid succession of damning news reports revealed multiple affairs, including one with a woman that US intelligence says is a Chinese spy and others with employees. The scandal is unequivocally damaging for Huang. And, at least in the short term, destabilizing for Nvidia, and detrimental to the AI trade , Yahoo Finance's Hamza Shaban writes:
The key-person risk extended to the entire AI trade. Huang was everywhere, seemingly… If Nvidia was the "central bank of AI," Huang was the chair.
But if Nvidia and the broader AI trade successfully weather the storm , it could amount to a huge win for both the company and sector.
Bitcoin ( BTC ) fell below $70,000 for the first time in nearly three months early Friday as investors weigh the largest cryptocurrency's value against a more hawkish Federal Reserve and other mounting headwinds.
After dropping to $68,000, bitcoin recovered to around $69,265, leaving it down more than 10% so far in November, according to Yahoo Finance data.
The latest decline follows a Wednesday decision by major index provider MSCI's to remove Michael Saylor's Strategy ( MSTR ), the largest publicly traded corporate holder of bitcoin, from two US stock indexes. That move could force funds tracking those benchmarks to sell shares of the company.
But bitcoin's troubles extend well beyond Strategy.
"The latest selloff is being driven by a combination of macro risk aversion, persistent spot Bitcoin ETF outflows, and an unwind of leveraged long positions," said Lacie Zhang, analyst at crypto firm Bitget.
Expectations for further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes have weighed on riskier assets, especially bitcoin, while weakness in technology stocks has added to the pressure.
Crypto-related stocks including Coinbase Global ( COIN ), Robinhood ( HOOD ) and Circle Internet Group ( CRCL ) also declined early Friday.
Yahoo Finance's Jared Blikre reports:
Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock went into free fall Thursday as CEO Jensen Huang stepped down, and retail investors were there to catch it. The question now is whether they bought the bottom or just the first leg down.
Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO after reports of two affairs , and CFO Colette Kress is stepping in as interim CEO. The stock fell as much as 14% at the open to its lowest level since June 2025, then clawed back nearly three-quarters of it to close down about 4%. Nvidia reports earnings Tuesday with no permanent CEO in sight.
Small investors bought a net $111 million of Nvidia stock in the first 30 minutes of trading. According to Vanda Research, that was the stock's biggest opening on record and more than 40 times a normal start. Nvidia has soaked up 61% of all retail buying in US stocks and ETFs this week. Money also poured into leveraged funds betting on Nvidia gains, while funds betting against it drew nothing.
"This is very much a one-way flow story for retail," Vanda wrote.
Mike Zaccardi, a CFA and CMT, called it "one of the more epic 'buy the news' events in history" on X.

articles.title_orig: How the Microsoft outage has been felt worldwide
articles.title_zh: How the Microsoft outage has been felt worldwide
articles.content_orig:
At least 74 countries have been affected by the Microsoft outage since it was detected after midday US Eastern Time (17:00 GMT) on Thursday.
Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and artificial intelligence software Copilot, are experiencing "connectivity problems", the company said.
From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, disruption has been widespread. Here's what's been happening around the world.
In the US , staff with the House of Representatives told Politico their work had been halted by the outage.
"We all use Outlook, that's our life, everything is there, our calendar is there, our boss's calendar, so it has been a challenge … with no access to our Bible," one House staff member said. "There goes a day of legislative work."
Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic have both reported problems.
OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which caused some tools not to work as expected.
Courts from Los Angeles to Texas also warned that communications might be delayed.
Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on 12 November, rescheduled to 16 November, citing business disruptions caused by the outage.
Meanwhile, officials in some US cities encouraged citizens to call local offices and agencies where needed instead of using email.
The City of Austin in Texas account posted on X early on Friday: "Due to an ongoing Microsoft Outlook outage, City of Austin employees cannot receive or send emails at this time.
"City phone lines remain operational, and 911 Emergency services are not impacted."
In Canada , the public broadcaster CBC reported that a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto had declared a code grey, indicating an infrastructure failure.
The company, Unity Health Toronto, said its teams were having trouble sending or receiving email but that patient care was not affected.
In Japan , some companies reportedly turned to fax machines to maintain communications.
"Can't send emails because of a Microsoft outage, so we're switching to fax for the regular updates we usually send as PDFs. Analog is strong," one unnamed X user was quoted as saying by the Japan Times .
The Japanese government said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.
"We understand that Microsoft is working to restore services, and we will continue to monitor the company's response," Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki told reporters.
Singapore also confirmed the outage had affected some government systems, but stressed "emergency services remain fully operational".
Singapore's courts also said they were "experiencing issues with incoming and outgoing emails", urging people to contact them by telephone for urgent matters.
In the Philippines , the Supreme Court warned that "responses to emails and other transactions may be delayed".
In India , the outage was disrupting work for many on Friday, with emails not landing and Teams calls not going through smoothly.
People working in the equity markets told BBC News they had panicked when they realised they could not access daily research reports before their morning meeting where they make their big decisions of the day.
"Outlook wasn't working. We fortunately have an alternative so it was not a problem. But we conduct most of our calls, especially with big clients, on Teams - that has been a challenge," a senior executive with a big Indian brokerage said on condition of anonymity.
Firms in China use software that has been made locally - WPS Office is a favourite - but the Microsoft outage caused frustration there too.
Outlook is one of the few reliable channels for many offices and businesses in the country who work with colleagues across the world.
China operates one of the world's most sophisticated systems of internet censorship, known as the Great Firewall, which restricts access to many Western websites including Google, Facebook and Instagram along with many international news organisations including the BBC.
Australia's spy and federal police agencies have been affected by the outage, though officials have suggested the impact is minimal.
"The impact that they are dealing with is very much on email system", the head of the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation, Mike Burgess, told reporters.
Other Australian public service providers also confirmed they had been affected by the outage, but similarly said this was mostly limited to emails, and the BBC understands there were no major impacts across New South Wales' primary services in health, education, transport, and emergency services.
European stock market operator Euronext advised listed companies on Friday morning to use the phone to communicate corporate information because of the Outlook email disruption, Reuters reports.
In the UK , GPs, police and pharmacies are among services affected.
Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report.
Politicians are also affected. At Westminster, MPs were reporting their access via parliamentary accounts to Microsoft products was down.
A parliamentary spokesperson said: "We are aware of the global issue affecting Microsoft email services, which is impacting users of the parliamentary network. We are working with Microsoft to resolve the matter as quickly as possible.
"Alternative communication arrangements are in place, allowing today's business to continue."
Some parts of Asia, Europe and Africa remain unaffected, according to Downdetector. These include Russia, where the use of Microsoft applications is heavily restricted, or phased out in favour of domestic alternatives.
However, this could also be a case of under-reporting in some countries, where Downdetector is among the websites blocked due to censorship.

articles.title_orig: Treasury Yield Surge Shatters Hopes Worst of Bond Rout Is Over
articles.title_zh: Treasury Yield Surge Shatters Hopes Worst of Bond Rout Is Over
articles.content_orig:
Treasury yields edged higher on Friday as investor expectations for a December rate hike by the Federal Reserve gathered strength.
The 10-year U.S. Treasury note yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — rose 2 basis points to 5.1271%.
The longer-dated 30-year Treasury bond yield, which tends to react to geopolitical risks, was 3 basis points higher at 5.4602%. The 2-year Treasury note yield, which is typically more sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was 1 basis point lower at 4.8525%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
The upward moves come after 10-year Treasury yields jumped more than 13 basis points to more than 5% during Thursday's session , and the 2-year yield soared more than 15 basis points.
Investors now see a Federal Reserve rate hike next month as a near certainty. Traders are pricing in 100% odds of a rise at the Dec. 9 meeting, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Odds of a 25 basis points hike now stand at almost 87%, with the chance of a 50 basis point increase at around 13%.
Energy inflation remains in focus, with oil set for its second weekly decline as the prospects of renewed strikes by the U.S. against Iran recede. Prices were choppy in early trade Friday. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for December delivery were down 0.1% at $88.63 per barrel. Brent crude was higher by 0.3% at $96.11.
October's producer price index — a key measure of wholesale inflation — is due later Friday. It is expected to show 0.4% growth for last month, compared to 1.3% in September's report.

articles.title_orig: Europe pushes for seat at Ukraine peace talks‌ but lacks unified voice
articles.title_zh: Europe pushes for seat at Ukraine peace talks‌ but lacks unified voice
articles.content_orig:
European leaders have waited on the margins of negotiations to end Russia’s war in Ukraine for months, eyeing a seat at the table. Now they finally expect to get one, and they don’t know who should sit in it.
“If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation,” Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and a U.S. envoy, said on Thursday.
Mr. Kushner’s dig reflected a harsh — and, for Europe, potentially embarrassing — reality that internal divisions could cost European officials time and influence. Mr. Kushner and his fellow U.S. negotiator, Steve Witkoff, pushed this week to add Europe to the talks after Russia insisted during discussions in the United Arab Emirates that postwar security in Europe be a topic of negotiation.
Russian negotiators made it clear during the talks with Ukraine and the United States that as a condition of ending the war, they want Europe to change how it protects itself. Russia has a record of pushing to pare back NATO operations near its border.
European officials have rejected those suggestions, insisting that the continent, not the Kremlin, decides its security.

articles.title_orig: After Xi Purges China’s Generals, a Military Inquisitor Rises
articles.title_zh: After Xi Purges China’s Generals, a Military Inquisitor Rises
articles.content_orig:
When China’s leader, Xi Jinping, endorsed the expulsion of dozens of disgraced officials at a recent Communist Party meeting in Beijing, one man stood out as a clear winner.
Taking his new place at the front of the meeting was Gen. Zhang Shengmin, the somber-faced enforcer of Mr. Xi’s purges inside the military. He had been promoted to the Politburo, the party’s top leadership council, the latest step in his improbable rise from low-profile inspector to a position second only to Mr. Xi in China’s military hierarchy.
General Zhang has been the principal overseer of Mr. Xi’s campaign to purify the People’s Liberation Army. His latest elevation signaled that the investigations, indoctrination drives and loyalty tests could continue for years, as Mr. Xi searches for officers he believes are irreproachably loyal, experts and officials said.
“Twist the blade inward, with strict measures to cure disorder,” China’s main military newspaper said after the party meeting that was held late last month, referring to the continued discipline campaign.
Three officials in Taiwan said they believed Mr. Xi’s loyalty campaign would keep the Chinese military focused on its own problems. That could hinder preparations for possible war over Taiwan, the self-governed island democracy that Beijing claims. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal assessments.
The leadership uncertainty comes as China’s military has continued to pressure Taiwan. Dozens of P.L.A. ships held unannounced drills in seas off the Chinese coast in recent weeks, with some, including a carrier strike group, still remaining, Joseph Wu , the secretary-general of Taiwan’s National Security Council, posted on X on Thursday.

articles.title_orig: Study Hard, Get a Career and Get Ahead? It’s Not What It Used to Be.
articles.title_zh: Study Hard, Get a Career and Get Ahead? It’s Not What It Used to Be.
articles.content_orig:
Protest movements have long relied on students as some of the most ardent foot soldiers. Young people have been on the front lines of protests against war, climate change and racial inequality. But in huge protests that have shaken India and France this fall, students have revolted against the failed promises of education itself.
In India, students took to the streets after the government abruptly canceled the results of a medical-school admissions exam because test questions had been leaked online. Aspiring doctors had to take the test again, after many spent years studying for up to 12 hours a day in hopes of winning one of the coveted spots — and the chance of upward mobility. Young people across the country saw the scandal as emblematic of a broken education system and were furious.
In France, students in poor suburbs outside Paris began protesting the decrepit physical condition of their schools, an opaque university admissions system and absent teachers. French education had long promised to serve as a “social elevator” enabling young people to advance in society, but had fallen into disrepair. Soon, demonstrations spread across the country and, in some cities, spiraled into rioting.
In both countries, the anger of the students shows no signs of abating. And while in many ways France and India could hardly be more different, their unrest was sparked by a similar source of outrage: the breakdown of a foundational social contract that one could call the meritocratic bargain.
It is a promise that lies at the core of many countries’ political compacts. Though specifics can vary, the central proposition usually goes something like this: A fair society rewards merit. Educational achievements are a good measure of merit because education is open to all and leads to valuable skills. Therefore, education should be a route to social and economic advancement.
The value of this system is not just that it selects for those with high ability, but also that it offers a justification for the resulting socioeconomic hierarchy — including who ends up at the bottom. “All selection mechanisms generate losers,” said Nicholas Kuipers, a professor at Princeton University who studies the politics of meritocracy. “The question is, Who do you want to be a loser, and who do you want to be a winner?”

articles.title_orig: Alice Huang-Linked Firm Procured Banned Nvidia Chips in China
articles.title_zh: Alice Huang-Linked Firm Procured Banned Nvidia Chips in China
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The cheapest way for an American company to run AI is a free model made in China. The scandal that just cost Nvidia its CEO could shut off the chips those models depend on.
Companies are making the switch fast. Duolingo ( DUOL ) co-founder and CEO Luis von Ahn said at Yahoo Finance Invest on Thursday that each AI practice call in his app used to cost about 30 cents. Now it's "less than a cent," he said, "by moving most of this to open weight models ," the kind of AI anyone can download and run for free. Decagon co-founder and CEO Jesse Zhang said new customers at his AI startup run "almost entirely" on them.
The most downloaded of those free models come from China, and the biggest maker by far is Alibaba ( BABA ).
Economist Nouriel Roubini says China's edge rests on two shortcuts that are closing fast. Chinese open models are about 95% as good as American ones, the NYU Stern professor emeritus said at Invest, because "we allowed distillation — that's over — and we allowed them through Singapore to get all these advanced chips." Distillation is when one AI model learns by copying a stronger model's answers.
Alibaba stock fell 7% Thursday to its lowest close since January 2025 as reports circulated that Washington is moving to shut down that Singapore route. The company reports earnings Nov. 19.
Alibaba's free AI models, called Qwen, get about half of the downloads that can be traced to a maker on Hugging Face , the biggest online library of AI models, by Yahoo Finance calculations. That's more than twice as many as Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ), OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ), Meta ( META ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), and Nvidia ( NVDA ) combined.
"Right now there is massive usage of ... a Chinese family called Qwen, which is the most used one," Hugging Face co-founder Thomas Wolf said on Deirdre Bosa Live this week.
Meta used to own this race. Its Llama 4 and Alibaba's Qwen3 came out the same month in 2025. Developers have since downloaded Qwen3 more than 20 times as often on Ollama, a popular app for running AI on your own computer.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after admitting to an affair with a woman US intelligence officials believe passed information to Beijing, according to reports . She has been identified as Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore company that rents out computing power built on Nvidia chips.
Alibaba was Megaspeed's founding customer and is still its biggest, the Financial Times reported . The US investigation targets Megaspeed, not Alibaba, and Megaspeed denies diverting chips.
China can't legally buy Nvidia's most advanced chips, so renting them abroad has been the workaround. Now the Commerce Department is finalizing a rule that would bar Chinese AI companies from using advanced chips in data centers outside China, including in Singapore and Malaysia, The Information reported .
The scandal also cost America's open-source AI its loudest booster. "Jensen was a great champion for open weight," Zhang said, adding that "there's still a gap between the open-source frontier in the US and in China." And China hawks in Washington now have an opening to press their case.
Roubini thinks Washington's crackdown will flip that gap. Without copying American models and without the Singapore chips, he said, China's AI makers are "going to lag behind us."

articles.title_orig: Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories
articles.title_zh: Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories
articles.content_orig:
If schools don't want Google AI Overviews to appear when students use its flagship Search tool, the company said, they will lose access to Google Search altogether. Don Ryan/AP/AP hide caption
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
Google is a big part of the school day for millions of students. It's not only a search engine. It's a hub for sharing documents and turning in homework.
An announcement this month makes it clear: Google wants AI to be a part of that education ecosystem.
"Parents are angry," said Jodi Carreon, a mom in Southern California. "They're very angry."
When Carreon, who also runs the advocacy group Schools Beyond Screens , first read that Google was letting schools turn off AI features for students, she was excited. Her group is part of the parent-led movement demanding limits on technology in the classroom .
But even as districts including Los Angeles Unified , Seattle Public Schools and New York City Public Schools recently agreed to bans on AI in the classroom, Google did not. If schools don't want AI Overviews to appear when students use its flagship Search tool, the company said, they will lose access to Google Search altogether. Even advocates who want less tech in schools know losing the ability to "Google" something will be an issue for teachers.
In a post on X , New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Google is using "its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools," and Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts wrote to Google's CEO demanding the company reverse its policy.
Tracy Pizzo worked at Google for more than a decade before leaving the company in 2022. Much of her time at the company was focused on education and ethical AI standards. Google's move this month baffled her, especially coming at a time when young people's use of AI is under such scrutiny.
She has a theory about why the tech giant is taking this stance: It could be linked to two recent court cases Google fended off in D.C.
Google was sued by big online publishers who said adding AI overview to search negatively affected their business. The publishers sued under antitrust laws, and their argument hinged on convincing the court that AI Overviews was a separate product from Google Search.
"The judge decided that Search and AI are an integrated product," Pizzo said, and subsequently dismissed the cases. "Now if Google were to provide an off switch for schools only … that's evidence that they can be separated. And that undermines the win they just had in court."
When asked for comment, Google directed NPR to its original announcement , where the company said, "Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit." The company did not respond to additional questions by NPR about any connection between its announcement and recent antitrust cases.
NPR asked antitrust experts about this theory. They weren't entirely convinced, but also didn't dismiss it altogether.
In any case, Google's AI Overviews doesn't get high marks from some watchdogs.
Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that evaluates how teens interact with technology, recently gave the product an " unacceptable risk " rating. Among other things, Common Sense dinged the tool for unsafe content and citing false information.
The day after the announcement, Google came under fire for another AI product in schools. Parents in North Carolina sued the company after Google's chatbot, Gemini, helped their 13-year-old daughter plan her suicide and funeral on her school-issued Chromebook.
Even some of Google's longtime partners are surprised by the company's current position, including superintendent Hank Thiele in Illinois.
"It may have caused a lot of damage in the trust that Google has built in education," he said.
Thiele has worked with Google Classroom for almost two decades and says the company has always been a great partner. His district, made up entirely of high school students, is in the process of figuring out AI for its students. As an early adopter of tech in the classroom, he wants to be on top of it with AI.
He said he thinks the company will listen to people's feedback but they bungled the messaging.
"Google should have just plainly said, 'Our bad,'" Thiele said. "That would have been the appropriate response to a school."
The "AI or nothing" approach, as Thiele put it, did not land well.

articles.title_orig: The U.S.-Israel Relationship Is Broken. Here’s How Eisenkot Could Fix It.
articles.title_zh: The U.S.-Israel Relationship Is Broken. Here’s How Eisenkot Could Fix It.
articles.content_orig:
Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief who has been given a chance to form Israel’s new governing coalition and replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is by no means assured of success.
But if he does take power, another hugely daunting challenge would immediately confront him: how to undo the vast damage done to Israel’s relationship with the United States, its closest and most important ally.
It’s hard to imagine things getting much worse.
Many Americans have turned against Israel over its devastating military campaign in Gaza, and even more so over its role in pressing for war with Iran , which led to soaring gas prices.
President Trump announced this month that he would cut off billions of dollars in annual U.S. military aid to Israel by the end of the year and blamed Israel in part for Republican losses in the midterm elections. Democratic control of Congress could quickly lead to sanctions on violent Israeli settlers and on new settlement construction in the occupied West Bank, as well as to new conditions on arms sales.
In the past, Israel could always turn to Congress for support in clashes with the White House, said Michael Oren, a former Israeli ambassador to Washington and deputy prime minister under Mr. Netanyahu. But no longer.
“For the first time in the history of our relationship with the United States, we have no recourse,” he said. “We have to start from scratch. We have a lot of fence mending to do and with no guarantee of success. Zero.”

articles.title_zh: Trump's reliance on ousted Nvidia CEO in question ahead of China trip
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Jensen Huang, the billionaire co-founder of tech firm Nvidia, resigned as CEO after allegations of extramarital affairs including with an alleged Chinese spy rocked his company.
The 63-year-old’s departure comes in the wake of a scandal that has wiped an estimated $500 billion off the chipmaker’s market value , with share prices plunging 12 percent to start Thursday. However, they have rebounded some ad were down 5 percent by midday.
One of the world’s richest men, Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993, which is now at the heart of the AI revolution. He is the company’s fourth-largest investor with a stake of about 3.61 percent, and will exit the Nvidia board with immediate effect, the company announced Thursday.
“Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” Nvidia said in a statement.
U.S. President Donald Trump, who is close to Huang , suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook should replace him.
“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump posted Thursday on Truth Social. “A Legend replaces a Legend!”
When the board announced Huang’s resignation early Thursday it also stated that Colette Kress, Nvidia’s executive vice president and chief financial officer, would serve as interim CEO.
“The Board, Estaff (executive staff) and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period,” Kress wrote in a memo to employees, adding the company will host a meeting on November 18.
Huang’s problems began when The New York Times reported he had had an affair with former Megaspeed director Alice Huang — no relation — whom U.S. intelligence has said facilitated shipments of Nvidia’s microchips to Chinese firms as part of a foreign intelligence operation.
The newspaper subsequently alleged that the executive had also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell , his company’s vice president of healthcare, who is also married.
After the first of the infidelities was disclosed, the executive sent a memo to Nvidia employees Sunday admitting he had been unfaithful to his wife of 40 years , Lori Huang, and said he was “deeply sorry” for the hurt he had case without going into details. Nvidia’s board responded by launching an internal investigation .
China meanwhile denied the espionage claims, calling them “purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China.”
Huang’s exit creates a leadership vacuum at the $4 trillion chipmaker, that is the driving force behind the global AI boom and at the heart of the big tech arms race between the U.S. and China .
For years, Nvidia was best known to video gamers for helping produce top-tier graphics. But its chips' ability to perform many calculations at once has made them a strategic prize in the US-China race to dominate AI technology. It also made Nvidia the world's most valuable company.
The success turned Huang into a rock-star CEO, mobbed by fans in Taiwan and South Korea who would ask him to sign books, posters and even their bodies.
Prior to the announcement, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, an expert on corporate governance at Yale School of Management, told NBC News the scandal meant Huang had “lost his legitimacy to lead internally in the eyes of the company, and he’s lost his external credibility in the eyes of key constituents, including customers.”
Before the resignation, fellow tech boss Elon Musk said it would be “an honor” to hire Huang, the pair having previously worked together on Tesla, xAI and space-based data center projects.
The world’s richest man recently said of Huang, “old friends are the best friends,” adding: “Jensen rocks.”
It is not yet clear whether Huang’s extramarital affairs will end his marriage. Forbes has estimated Lori Huang could receive a windfall of at least $75 billion if the couple does divorce, putting her in an exclusive tech billionaire ex-wives’ club that also includes Melinda French Gates and MacKenzie Scott.
The scandal has also reverberated in Washington, D.C., with reports that Trump was warned about Huang’s compromised position by Secretary of State Marco Rubio in May when the executive joined their visit to Beijing.
Earlier this week, Trump said he had “absolutely no idea” that the first reported affair was with a suspected Chinese spy.
“I think ​he's an honorable guy," Trump said, adding ​that Huang had “done an amazing job for our country.”
Republican leaders of three House committees have meanwhile called for Huang to deliver closed-door testimony on his interactions with the alleged intelligence asset. Democratic senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons have written to Trump’s commerce secretary Howard Lutnick to demand that all company records relating to Nvidia’s dealings with China be preserved.
Nvidia has started a search for a new permanent CEO and said it had full confidence in Kress, the interim leader.
“Colette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Harvey Jones, chair of Nvidia’s board of directors.
“The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”
Rhian Lubin contributed to this report from New York

articles.title_orig: The AI boom was built around Jensen Huang. Now what?
articles.title_zh: The AI boom was built around Jensen Huang. Now what?
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia in scandal leaves the company without its visionary leader. It also leaves a major void for the AI industry, where Huang was kingmaker in inking deals to support the tech boom.
Under Huang’s leadership, Nvidia became more than a chipmaker: It guaranteed deals for data centers, invested heavily in AI startups and even backed the companies that bought its products.
Huang put Nvidia at the core of AI financing, and the CEO himself championed some of the industry’s biggest deals. His departure puts a spotlight on whether the ecosystem he crafted could fracture — and whether that would spell trouble for the AI boom that has helped prop up the US stock market and become a driving force of economic growth.
“It’s hard to overstate his personal role in all of this,” said Neil Wilson, a strategist at investment bank Saxo.
“Huang was key in Nvidia being the backer of last resort across the AI ecosystem, really underpinning a lot of the financing and infrastructure guarantees,” he said.
Nvidia backstopped deals, like committing $105 billion in August for an OpenAI data center. The company has a major equity stake in the neocloud CoreWeave, emerging as an important financial backer and confidence booster. Nvidia is expected to take a $10 billion stake in Anthropic’s initial public offering.
Nvidia makes the graphics processing units that power AI models like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude. But the company has also been “the central bank of AI,” Jay Goldberg, senior analyst at Seaport Research Partners, told CNN.
The company also functions like a venture capitalist, Goldberg noted, investing in companies to fuel their growth and help them get ahead in an industry that requires massive amounts of capital.
“Circular financing” has emerged as a term to describe Nvidia’s financial agreements, because the company is backing the companies that, in turn, buy its products. Goldberg said a more accurate term would be “very aggressive vendor financing.”
The company’s financial commitments in the AI boom have grown to the point that it had to address the associated risks in its latest quarterly earnings filing.
“Commitments, guarantees and other commercial arrangements expose us to financial, counterparty and execution risks and may not provide anticipated benefits,” Nvidia said in its most recent quarterly earnings report.
Huang’s sudden fall from grace puts that financing strategy in question. He resigned amid revelations extramarital affairs and a board investigation into whether he was the target of a “foreign intelligence effort.”
Just three months ago, after committing the $105 billion for the OpenAI data center, Huang brought together six major financial institutions — Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR — to agree to treat Nvidia’s AI infrastructure as an asset class to write debt against, with aims of mobilizing over $500 billion for the AI boom.
“That was all driven by [Huang],” Goldberg said, adding that the deal isn’t finalized, and he expects it will come under additional review (and could even fall through).
Jensen Huang is living proof that AI’s rockstar CEOs are also a hidden risk
Nvidia’s central role in AI financing is directly related to the so-called neoclouds, or companies that rent out compute to power the boom.
Nvidia, as the primary provider of technology to power AI, has reaped massive profits in recent years. The company has used its cash to invest in neoclouds like CoreWeave and also provide backstops by guaranteeing to step in and provide revenue if they can’t sell all the compute capacity from Nvidia’s GPUs.
If Nvidia loses its savvy as an AI financier, it muddies the outlook for the neocloud industry, which relies on Nvidia as a bedrock to help issue those guarantees that help companies lock in more affordable interest rates.
In October, when CoreWeave’s bond yields spiked, the situation only calmed after Huang stepped in and expressed confidence in the company’s future. “I’m optimistic,” Huang told Bloomberg News on October 15. CoreWeave stock rallied 6% that day, snapping a three-day slide.
“This just raises the pressure on some of the smaller neoclouds’ ability to raise capital,” Goldberg said.
“When we lose Jensen, we lose a lot of the animating force that’s been driving the industry,” Goldberg said. “So, the world just feels a little bit smaller without him.”
Huang’s financing strategy not only supports the growth of the AI boom, but effectively secured Nvidia’s status as the axis on which everything was connected.
The AI industry’s existing long-term agreements mean the near-term outlook likely stays the same, Goldberg said. But, over time, Nvidia’s ability to deploy the same creative financing strategies could become less certain and potentially slow the industry’s expansion.
While Nvidia announced Thursday that Colette Kress, the chief financial officer, would be interim CEO, potentially reassuring investors, replacing Huang’s dealmaking expertise will be a much bigger challenge.
“He was not only the chief technology architect … but he was also the capital allocator,” Ted Mortonson, tech strategist at Baird, told CNN.
“With him leaving, it leaves a huge void,” Mortonson said.
Nvidia also faces competition for its role as the core provider of compute, with other semiconductor companies like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom already building alternatives to the company’s GPUs.
Uncertainty over Nvidia’s role could put pressure on other tech companies, or the hyperscalers like Alphabet and Amazon, to step up as the capital allocator Nvidia has been. But it remains to be seen who can champion the industry and execute dealmaking like Huang.
Huang’s dual role as the man who understood the tech and the dealmaker who understood the financing was a unique combination that contributed to his star-status role, Mortonson said.
Huang gave Nvidia the clout and ability to dictate terms on pricing and deals, analysts said. Without Huang, that ability becomes less apparent.
“Jensen’s successor will not have the same latitude or deference to pursue circular deals and pursue aggressive sales tactics,” Mike O’Rourke, chief market strategist at JonesTrading, told CNN in an email.
“There’s the quantifiable and the unquantifiable,” said Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of the Founders 100 ETF, a fund focused on founder-led companies.
“There are things you can’t put in a spreadsheet, right?,” Monaghan said. “He has that aura, plus all of that engineering knowledge, plus all of the 33 years of building all this stuff. You just can’t replace that.”
“Jensen knew where to put his own capital to help grow the ecosystem, and that walks out the door with him,” Monaghan said.
Demand for AI is robust. Anthropic’s revenue in the third quarter soared more than 1,000% year-over-year, a sign that people are adopting and paying for AI. Companies are likely to keep investing in infrastructure to meet the demand. But investors ultimately want to see those investment turn into profits, or may begin to question whether the massive spending is justified.
Huang’s departure shakes the foundation of the sprawling web of financing that has come to define the AI economy. A slowdown in dealmaking could exacerbate cost pressures, spell trouble for smaller companies and create added headwinds that could hamper the AI trade.
“The risk is less about chip demand than about the money,” David Rosenberg, president and founder at Rosenberg Research, wrote in a note. “Nvidia’s stakes, guarantees and backstops are what tie the AI trade together, so the weakest links are the borrowers who depend on Nvidia’s support.”

Asian airlines are facing expiring jet fuel hedge contracts and need to make a choice about whether to hedge at exorbitant prices or risk them going even higher without a hedge.
Citing industry executives, Reuters reported today that jet fuel prices in Asia are currently about 75% higher than they were before the war in the Middle East started, and that the chance of that changing dramatically in the observable future appears to be slim.
“Our view is that we are facing a new normal where the fuel price is there to stay at the levels that we see more or less today,” the chief executive of Kazakhstan’s Air Astana told Reuters.
This view would support a pro-hedge stance, to insure against prices going even higher—but not everyone is happy about this, not at current jet fuel price levels. Said levels are off October peaks that reached close to $180 per barrel, but at $148 per barrel are still quite high.
Jet fuel costs now represent 33% of an airline’s operating costs, according to Wong Hong, the director general of the Association of Asia Pacific Airlines. Before the war, the share of jet fuel in airlines’ operating costs, per the International Air Transport Association, stood at 25%. As a result, airlines that are facing the expiration of their latest hedge contracts are also facing a “very, very tricky dilemma,” according to Hong.
Not everyone is as pessimistic, however. “We still think it will be cyclical. It's going to go up and down,” Japan Airlines senior managing executive officer Ross Leggett told Reuters. Despite this, Japan Airlines is budgeting for a worst-case scenario with jet fuel at $160 per barrel. This is the price that the airline had to pay for its fuel between April and September.
All airlines globally are struggling with the impact of the Middle East war on jet fuel prices. Sharp drops in profitability and plans to raise ticket prices are among the first-order effects.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia without Jensen Huang. What lies ahead for Asian chipmakers?
articles.title_zh: Nvidia without Jensen Huang. What lies ahead for Asian chipmakers?
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia's leadership shake-up is unlikely to cause immediate disruption for major Asian semiconductor suppliers, such as Samsung Electronics and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., but Jensen Huang's departure has raised questions about the company's longer-term product strategy and supply chain relationships.
The bigger issue for investors and suppliers is whether Nvidia can maintain the pace of innovation and close ties with key partners that Huang helped drive as the company built its dominance in artificial intelligence chips.
In a Friday research note, Nam Dae-jong and Kim Yeon-mi, analysts at South Korean brokerage Daol Investment & Securities, said Huang's departure was unlikely to affect the semiconductor industry's near-term outlook.
However, they flagged uncertainty over Nvidia's medium- to long-term product roadmap, including how its new leadership would coordinate with partners across the AI ecosystem.
For chipmakers in Asia, one key question is whether Nvidia's relationships with its manufacturing partners could change under new leadership.
Nam and Kim expect Nvidia's foundry relationship with TSMC to remain unchanged, given the companies' established partnership.
They also expect Nvidia's relationship with Samsung's foundry business to continue, citing growing cooperation between the companies, including manufacturing involving Samsung's 4-nanometer process and work on next-generation high-bandwidth memory technology.
The analysts said custom AI chips, or application-specific integrated circuits, or ASICs, are emerging as alternatives to Nvidia's graphic processing units and could accelerate diversification in the AI chip market.
However, they cautioned against interpreting growing competition as a sign of weakening demand for memory semiconductors, particularly high-bandwidth memory, or HBM.
Still, uncertainty remains over Nvidia's longer-term product roadmap, given Huang's central role in shaping the company's business strategy and allocating resources.
SK Hynix, another key supplier to Nvidia, reversed earlier gains to close 3.03% lower on Friday.
In a research note earlier in the day, Shinhan Securities said investors had initially looked past concerns over Nvidia's leadership change and focused instead on the broader outlook for the AI industry.
South Korea's Kospi also reversed earlier gains Friday. In a research note, iM Securities said the impact of Nvidia's leadership change on the broader semiconductor sector appeared limited, pointing to gains in AMD and Broadcom shares in the previous U.S. session and continued investment demand for AI companies.
ASUS Co-CEO S.Y. Hsu told CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia " that Nvidia's leadership change was unlikely to alter its competitive advantages in the near term, though the company would monitor any impact on product quality, service costs and deliveries.
"I think Nvidia's product and the total AI ecosystem, the advantage will not change overnight," Hsu said.
ASUS, which works with Nvidia across graphics cards and AI servers, has yet to interact with interim CEO Colette Kress, Hsu said, adding that the company was seeking a meeting to better understand any potential strategic changes.
Over the longer term, Hsu said Huang had played a key role in helping Nvidia and its partners accelerate innovation, and that he would be watching to see whether the company could maintain that pace without him.

articles.title_orig: Lutnick should have prevented the diversion of sensitive Nvidia AI chips to China, critics charge
articles.title_zh: Lutnick should have prevented the diversion of sensitive Nvidia AI chips to China, critics charge
articles.content_orig:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under fire from critics asking whether his ties to Chinese companies and friendship with Nvidia's ousted CEO Jensen Huang contributed to the federal agency's lack of oversight over billions in Nvidia AI chip sales, CBS has learned.
Before President Trump nominated Lutnick to lead the Commerce Department, Lutnick was the chairman and CEO of Cantor Fitzgerald, a New York investment bank which held about $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time.
Lutnick developed a warm relationship with Huang, who resigned Thursday as reports of a growing number of affairs caused new uncertainty about the world's dominant AI chipmaker. One of Huang's alleged relationships was with Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen Huang), who is believed by the U.S. to be a Chinese spy. She ran Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company that became one of Nvidia's biggest customers for AI chips and is suspected of illegally shipping Nvidia's most advanced AI chips to Chinese entities, circumventing a U.S. ban.
As commerce secretary, Lutnick took the helm of an agency responsible for policing exports of sensitive technology to adversaries and global rivals.
One way the Commerce Department keeps this information and technology out of the hands of China and other adversaries is by putting foreign companies and individuals on its Entity List . This restricts their ability to access U.S. technology products, and inclusion on the list means that the department believes there's a risk that the entity is involved in activities that are contrary to U.S. national security or foreign policy interests.
In 2024, under the Biden administration, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security launched an investigation into Nvidia's chip sales to Megaspeed to determine whether they were being redirected to China. But according to The New York Times , the probe was abruptly transferred to the Department of Justice. The Justice Department would not comment about the investigation.
The Commerce Department has not added a company to the Entity List since October 2025.
Last week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Lutnick over the Commerce Department's failure to place Megaspeed on the Entity List, Axios reported.
Chris McGuire, an expert on China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, said, "The real scandal here is the lack of enforcement of export controls."
He added that the Commerce Department had known for as long as a year that Megaspeed was being run by a woman who is believed by the U.S. to be a Chinese spy, "and they did nothing." The New York Times reported that about a year ago, President Trump was briefed on intelligence that suggested that Alice Huang was a Chinese asset and that she had grown close to Jensen Huang.
"Either Lutnick doesn't know how to do his job or he is protecting Huang," McGuire said.
The Commerce Department did not respond to a request for comment.
On Thursday, after Jensen Huang's resignation became public, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, called on Lutnick and his deputy, Jeffrey Kessler, to "explain why they have not closed export control loopholes." Kessler is the undersecretary who led the Commerce Department's probe into Megaspeed.
Warren urged the two to "act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military." In March, Warren wrote to Lutnick to demand the "immediate pausing" of all export licenses of Nvidia chips destined for China.
Questions about Lutnick's own relationship with Chinese state companies have further complicated the ongoing Nvidia crisis.
A financial services firm Lutnick ran, BGC Group, had a 33% stake in a joint venture with China Credit Trust, a Chinese state-owned company whose largest shareholder is the China People's Insurance Company, another state enterprise.
Another firm he ran, Cantor Fitzgerald, is still overseen by his two eldest sons. That firm helped several Chinese companies go public in the U.S. Cantor Fitzgerald was also a key investor in Satellogic, a satellite company that is under contract with a Chinese data science company, Zhong Ke Guang Qi Space, until 2033.
His close China ties emerged as a topic at his Senate confirmation hearing last year. Senators questioned whether he could be unduly influenced by Chinese officials, and how he would safeguard U.S. technology.
Sen. Maria Cantwell, a Democrat from Washington state, grilled Lutnick on potential conflicts of interest with respect to his investments in Chinese companies, and Cantor Fitzgerald's financial interest in Tether, a cryptocurrency company with a large footprint in China.
Other senators asked about how he would safeguard U.S. technology from the Chinese Communist Party.
"How will you address different threats that we see coming from the CCP within these information and technology markets?" asked GOP Sen. Deb Fischer, of Nebraska.
Lutnick promised to be vigilant against threats from China.
"I take a very jaundiced view of China," he said in response to Fischer. "I think they only care about themselves and seek harm to us, and so we need to protect ourselves."
Before he was sworn in as commerce secretary in February 2025, Lutnick resigned from all of his corporate leadership posts, transferring his business empire to his children.
Since his tenure as commerce secretary began, Lutnick and his family's net worth doubled to $7.3 billion, thanks to his indirect stake in Tether, according to Forbes , which valued his holding in Tether at $5.4 billion. The stake, worth $1.7 billion in early 2025, has more than tripled in value.
"Can we be confident that he is looking out for the public interest?" asked Kathleen Clark, a law professor and expert on government ethics at Washington University in St. Louis. "What's going on with him raises a lot of red flags."
Lutnick's friendship with Jensen Huang may also be problematic, Clark told CBS News.
Huang met Lutnick soon after Lutnick began his term as commerce secretary, Huang told podcaster Joe Rogan last year.
"He started our conversation with, 'Jensen, this is Secretary Lutnick,'" said Huang. "'I just want to let you know that you're a national treasure. Nvidia is a national treasure. And whenever you need access to the president, the administration, you call us.'"
Huang added that every time he called the commerce secretary's office, "if I want to get something off my chest, express some concern, they're always available."
Huang also visited with President Trump. He attended a $1 million-per-person dinner at Mar-a-Lago in April 2025. At that time, Huang tried to convince Mr. Trump to lift restrictions on the company's less advanced H20 chip sales to China, according to The New York Times . Less than three months later, in July 2025, Mr. Trump lifted the restrictions. Nvidia's most advanced chip, the Blackwell, still cannot be sold directly to China.
In July 2025, Lutnick posted a photo to Instagram showing Huang in his trademark black leather jacket standing in the Oval Office next to Mr. Trump, who was seated at his desk. Lutnick is also in the photo along with other visitors.
"Great to meet in the Oval Office with Jensen Huang on the very day Nvidia crossed $4 trillion in market cap," the post said.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine envoy row hijacks EU leaders’ first AI summit
articles.title_zh: Ukraine envoy row hijacks EU leaders’ first AI summit
articles.content_orig:
DUBLIN — It was supposed to all be about how Europe faces up to the challenges posed by artificial intelligence. Not for the first time at a summit of EU leaders, more pressing concerns are getting in the way.
The talks got started amid a global Microsoft outage, affecting services including Outlook and Teams across more than 70 countries, underscoring the exact dependencies on U.S. tech that leaders will be tackling in the day’s discussions.
And, as has so often been the case since Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, it’s that conflict which is set to dominate proceedings in Dublin.
The EU is at odds over who should represent it in any peace talks. When officials from Ukraine, Russia and the U.S. met in Abu Dhabi earlier this week, Europe was only on the fringes. Most European leaders say that must change ― but working out how and with whom is easier said than done.
Friday is the second day of meetings in the Irish capital. Thursday’s gathering of 50 leaders under the banner of the European Political Community included several discussions involving smaller groups, chats with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and a debrief from Donald Trump’s envoys who had earlier met Putin in Moscow. We’ll bring you the best of the action, from the latest on the Ukraine arguments to the AI discussions and other items which might crop up, like the race to succeed Christine Lagarde at the head of the European Central Bank and the never-ending back-and-forth over the EU’s next seven year budget.

articles.title_orig: After meeting Putin, U.S. envoys say Europe to join talks on ending Ukraine war
articles.title_zh: After meeting Putin, U.S. envoys say Europe to join talks on ending Ukraine war
articles.content_orig:
This blog is now closed. Read below for a roundup of news from two days of talks on Tuesday, November 10 and Wednesday, November 11:
This blog covering the trilateral Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi has now closed. Thank you for reading.
Join us on Thursday for fresh coverage as US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner separatelymeet with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte offered a characteristically upbeat appraisal of the talks in Abu Dhabi and the prospect of cracks emerging between European NATO members, Ukraine and Donald Trump's administration in the US.
"I was in touch with the NATO team present in Abu Dhabi in the last two days," he told reporters while on a visit to Norway. "What I am getting from those calls is that the US, Ukraine and Europe really being completely aligned and united."
However, he cautioned that "clearly we have to see that the Russian side is willing to play ball."
After more than a decade as prime minister of the Netherlands, Rutte has taken on the unenviable job of trying to keep NATO aligned and united more generally during Donald Trump's second term . He stepped into the role a matter of weeks before the 2024 presidential election in the US.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy landed in Dublin on Wednesday evening, as he and his team head to the ninth European Political Community Summit.
He said both bilateral and multilateral meetings were planned amid his visit to Ireland .
"I will take part in the opening plenary session of the EPC Summit. A meeting on diplomatic efforts with the American negotiating team — Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner — is also planned," he said on social media.
Kushner and Witkoff are first expected to head to Moscow from Abu Dhabi, before moving on to Dublin on Thursday.
The European Political Community is an intergovernmental forum for strategic discussions about the future of Europe. It was set up in 2022, in response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
The group's ninth summit is scheduled to start early on Thursday morning and to continue until roughly the end of the working day. Hosts Ireland are also the current holders of the EU's rotating presidency.
Kyrylo Budanov described the talks in Abu Dhabi as "tough."
"Ukraine's position remains unchanged," Volodymyr Zelenskyy's chief of staff said on Telegram.
"The war must be brought to a halt, and an effective security architecture must be established — on that ensures a lasting peace and makes any recurrence of Russian aggression impossible."
He said returning Ukrainian prisoners was a "specific focus" of the talks, seemingly a reference to the prisoner swap plans, saying "we have achieved a significant result in this regard."
Budanov also thanked US negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff "for their professionalism, persistence, and efforts in seeking solutions," and thanked the UAE for hosting the talks and supporting the process.
Russia's ambassador to the United States, Alexander Darchiev, has died "suddenly" at the age of 66, the Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday.
Darchiev was quite new in the job, having been appointed in March 2025 shortly after Donald Trump's return to the White House. From 2021 to 2024, he was ambassador to Canada.
The ministry called Darchiev an "outstanding diplomat, an experienced leader and a kind colleague."
It did not provide further details on the death.
Considered a specialist in US relations, Darchiev headed the Russian Foreign Ministry's North America department between 2014 and 2020 before graduating to ambassadorial roles.
When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, he called the move a "necessary measure."
Russia's chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky is quoted by state media as saying Moscow saw no possibility of exchanging territory with Ukraine as part of any potential agreement.
State news agency TASS quoted him saying there was "no possibility whatsoever for such exchanges."
TASS and Interfax also both cited Medinsky as saying that Russia had decided to establish a "security zone" along its border with Ukraine following the incursion into Kursk.
"This zone is already quite substantial, it is expanding — and will continue to expand," he said.
The reported comments did not make clear where Medinsky considered the border or the so-called buffer zones to be, quite possibly by design. Russia already claims large chunks of what the international community considers to be Ukraine as parts of its territory following its invasion.
Yuri Ushakov, a foreign policy advisor to Vladimir Putin and part of the Russian negotiating team, on Wednesday described the talks in Abu Dhabi as substantive and very useful.
Moscow's delegation is led by former Culture Minister Vladimir Medinsky, an another aide to Putin.
But Ushakov is also involved, along with deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabko and Mikhail Galuzin, and General Staff officers Igor Kostyukov and Yuri Shigarlovsky on the military side.
German government spokesman Stefan Kornelius has said that following the talks in Abu Dhabi, talks between Chancellor Friedrich Merz and President Vladimir Putin could become more likely.
Asked at a Berlin press conference whether Merz would be ready to speak with Putin, Kornelius said that during the talks in Abu Dhabi negotiators from Europe, the US and Ukraine — but not Russia — had reached an "understanding on the broad outlines."
"This understanding will now be shared with the Russian president. And on that basis, talks may ensue," Kornelius said.
This follows intimations from both sides that the German and Russian leaders might be ready to engage directly.
Russian state news agency Tass cited the Kremlin as saying that Putin would be open to talks with EU leaders including Merz, echoing comments made earlier this year .
Merz, meanwhile, had said last Friday that if Putin were to travel to December's G20 summit in Miami as rumored, he would not rule out a meeting.
Rustem Umerov, currently the head of Ukraine's foreign intelligence service and also its chief negotiator at the talks, also issued a statement following the roughly two hours of trilateral negotiations on Wednesday.
The former defense minister said negotiators discussed "achieving peace and post-war reconstruction," adding that "the first steps towards this must be an end to the war and security guarantees for Ukraine."
Over these two days, the parties were able to state their positions directly, and significant differences remain between them," Umerov said on Telegram.
"There is still a lot of difficult work ahead, but there are opportunities to continue the negotiation process."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had received a report on the Abu Dhabi talks from his negotiating team in Abu Dhabi.
He hailed an "important humanitarian arrangement regarding preparations for a new exchange," seemingly a reference to prisoner exchange plans. Zelenskyy also said negotiators discussed "their views on guaranteeing security" for Ukraine, as well as "broader formats for further work involving the Europeans" going forward.
Currently in Copenhagen in Denmark, Zelenskyy said his team would meet US negotiators in Dublin on Thursday, after they head to Moscow. But he also called for more European representation going forward.
"Ukraine's priority is to end the war as soon as possible with a dignified peace," Zelenskyy wrote on social media.
"We believe that Europe must be represented at every stage of real diplomacy. It is essential that the United States have a strong position and exert influence on the source of this war — that is Russia — so that Russia ends the war of its own making."
Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia praised "good momentum" after the two-day talks in Abu Dhabi.
"I think that we have a good momentum to bring the solution before the new year comes," Arakhamia said, adding that he hoped another session could be held "as soon as possible."
